stem: What is the correct order of the stages of the product life cycle after development?

options.rationale: Correct.
A product is introduced before it grows.
Growth comes before maturity.
Decline is the final stage.

stem: At which stage of the product life cycle are sales usually highest?

options.rationale: Correct: sales peak and level off in maturity.
Sales are low just after launch.
Sales are rising fast but have not yet peaked.
Sales are falling in decline.

explanation: Sales reach their peak in **maturity**, where they level off as the market becomes saturated.

stem: Why does a product usually make a loss in the introduction stage?

options.content: The price is always set below the cost of each unit
options.rationale: Price may be high (skimming) at introduction.

options.content: Sales are low while launch and promotion costs are high
options.rationale: Correct: revenue does not yet cover costs.

options.content: Competitors have already taken most of the market
options.rationale: There are few competitors at introduction.

options.content: The product is about to be withdrawn
options.rationale: That happens in decline.

explanation: Low sales and heavy launch costs (advertising, setting up distribution) usually mean a loss at introduction.

stem: A product's sales are high but have stopped increasing, and many rival brands are on sale. Which stage is the product in?

options.rationale: Sales would still be rising quickly.
Sales would be low with few rivals.
Correct: high, flat sales and strong competition.
Sales would be falling.

explanation: High but flat sales with many competitors indicate **maturity** (saturation).

stem: Which type of advertising is most typical of the introduction stage?

options.content: Reminder advertising for a product customers already know
options.rationale: That suits maturity.
A new product needs customers to know about it.

options.content: Informative advertising explaining what the product does
options.rationale: Correct: customers must learn about the new product.
That fits decline.

explanation: At introduction, customers do not know the product, so promotion **informs** them.

stem: A maker of maize snacks launches a new chilli flavour of its best-known snack, whose sales have levelled off. What is this?

options.rationale: Price has not changed.
The new flavour is not being tested in one area.
The product is being refreshed, not withdrawn.
Correct: changing the product delays decline.

explanation: A new flavour is an **extension strategy**: it renews interest and delays decline.
hints: Sales had levelled off: what is the business trying to do?

stem: Why does a business need products at different stages of the life cycle?

options.content: Products in decline make the highest profits
options.rationale: Profit is falling in decline.

options.content: Products at introduction need no finance
options.rationale: Launch is costly.

options.content: It stops any competitor from entering the market with rival products
options.rationale: A product range does not stop rivals.

options.content: Profits from mature products can pay for developing new ones
options.rationale: Correct: a balanced range keeps cash and profit flowing.

explanation: Mature products generate cash that funds the development and launch of new products; this keeps the business going when old products decline.
hints: Which stage produces the most cash, and which stage needs it?

stem: For which product would spending heavily on an extension strategy be least sensible?

options.content: A popular soft drink whose sales have been flat for two years
options.rationale: A new flavour or pack could revive sales.

options.content: A washing powder facing a new rival
options.rationale: New packaging or promotion could help.

options.content: A film camera whose users have switched to phone cameras
options.rationale: Correct: demand is disappearing; extension only wastes money.

options.content: A school-bag range in maturity facing new designs
options.rationale: A new design could extend its life.

explanation: Extension strategies only delay decline; when technology has replaced a product, it is usually better to invest in new products.
hints: Has the need for the product disappeared?

stem: In the decline stage, sales of a product fall.
explanation: True. Sales fall as customers switch to newer or better products.

stem: An extension strategy guarantees that a product will never decline.
explanation: False. Extension strategies only **delay** decline; eventually most products are replaced.

stem: Match each stage of the product life cycle with its typical feature.

right.content: Sales at their peak and levelling off
Low sales and usually a loss
Sales rising quickly and rivals entering

explanation: Sales rise slowly, then quickly, level off and then fall.

payload.template: When almost every customer who wants a product already has it, the market is said to be {{blank:a}}. Businesses then use {{blank:b}} strategies to delay decline.

explanation: Saturation occurs in maturity; extension strategies try to keep sales up.

stem: Name the stage of the product life cycle in which profit is usually highest.
explanation: Profit is usually highest in **maturity**, when sales are at their peak and launch costs have been recovered.

stem: Sales of a phone cover rose from 30,000 units in Year 2 to 72,000 units in Year 3. Calculate the percentage increase.
explanation: (72 − 30) ÷ 30 × 100 = 140%. Such rapid growth is typical of the growth stage.
workedSolution: 1. (72 − 30) ÷ 30 × 100 = 140%. Such rapid growth is typical of the growth stage.
hints: Divide the increase by the Year 2 figure.

stem: A soap manufacturer's best-selling bath soap has reached maturity. Explain **two** extension strategies it could use.

points.description: Strategy 1, e.g. new scent / version (antibacterial, for children).
Explained: gives customers a reason to buy again / attracts a new segment.
Strategy 2, e.g. new pack size, new markets (export, hotels), new promotion campaign.
Explained: reaches customers not buying now / renews interest, delaying decline.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It could launch an antibacterial version, which attracts families concerned about hygiene and renews interest in the brand. It could also sell a small, cheaper bar in tuck shops, reaching customers who cannot afford the full-size bar.

explanation: Extension strategies change the product, packaging, market, uses, promotion or price.
hints: Change the product, the pack, the market or the promotion.

stem:
Farai's company makes phone covers in Harare. Sales of its most popular cover are shown below.

| Year | Sales (thousand units) |
| --- | ---: |
| Year 1 | 8 |
| Year 2 | 30 |
| Year 3 | 72 |
| Year 4 | 95 |
| Year 5 | 97 |
| Year 6 | 81 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which stage of the product life cycle was the cover in between Year 2 and Year 3?

options.rationale: Introduction was Year 1, with low sales.
Correct: sales more than doubled.
Sales had not yet levelled off.
Sales were rising.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage fall in sales from Year 5 to Year 6, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain what stage the cover appears to be entering in Year 6 and **one** likely reason.

points.description: Decline.
Sales fell after levelling off in Years 4-5.
Reason, e.g. new phone models need different covers / rivals' cheaper or better covers.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Recommend whether Farai should use an extension strategy for the cover or replace it with a new design. Justify your answer.

points.description: Identifies a suitable extension strategy, e.g. new colours/ materials, price cut, new market.
Benefit: cheaper and less risky than a new design; customers know the brand.
Limitation: covers fit particular phone models; if those phones are out of date, extension wastes money.
New design: fits current phones, may restart growth; but development cost and risk.
Uses the data: fall of about 16% in one year after a peak.
Justified recommendation.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sales peaked at 97,000 and fell by 16.5% in Year 6. A new range of colours or a price cut would be cheap and might hold sales for a while. But phone covers fit particular phone models, and if people are replacing those phones, no extension strategy will stop the decline. Farai should design covers for the newest popular phones, using cash from the current cover while it still sells, and let the old cover decline with little extra spending.

explanation: (a) Growth. (b) 16.5%. (c) Decline. (d) A justified choice; a new design is likely better if the phones themselves are changing.
hints: (b) Divide the fall by the Year 5 figure.
(d) Ask whether the need for the product is disappearing.

stem: Rudo's company has sold "Zuva" orange squash in Zimbabwe for fifteen years. Sales have been flat for three years and several cheaper brands are now on sale. The marketing manager suggests two extension strategies: (1) launch a sugar-free version, or (2) start selling the squash in Zambia and Mozambique.

points.description: An action to extend the life of a product / stop sales falling.
Usually used in the maturity stage (e.g. new version, new market).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how the marketing mix for Zuva is likely to differ from the marketing mix used when it was first introduced.

points.description: Promotion: reminder rather than informative advertising.
Price: competitive / lower prices because of cheaper rivals (launch price may have been different).
Place: sold in many outlets now, few at launch.
Product: possibly new sizes or flavours added.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate which extension strategy Rudo's company should choose.

points.description: Sugar-free: attracts health-conscious customers; uses existing factory and distribution.
But may take sales from the original (cannibalisation) / development and testing cost.
Exports: new customers; spreads risk across countries.
But costs of transport, foreign regulations and currency; little knowledge of those markets.
Compares risk and cost of each.
Justified recommendation.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A sugar-free version uses the same factory, brand and distribution, so it is cheap to introduce and would attract health-conscious buyers who now avoid sugary drinks. It might take some sales from the original, but it also keeps those customers from switching to rivals. Exporting reaches many new customers, but transport, foreign rules and currency risks are high and the company knows little about those markets. Because the sugar-free version is cheaper and less risky and builds on the brand's strength at home, it should be the first choice, with exports considered later after market research.

explanation: In maturity the mix shifts to reminder promotion and competitive prices; the choice of extension strategy depends on cost and risk.
hints: (b) Compare promotion, price and place at introduction and maturity.
(c) Compare cost, risk and likely sales of each option.
